chapter: Will Marion Cook and the Southern Syncopated Orchestra
title: Tony Jackson and Cook's demand for feeling
summary: Briggs says Tony Jackson sounded good but he was busy following Cook's embellishments with lip slides; Cook valued heart above tuition.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: What the word "jazz" means: origins, Dixieland and labels

blocks.x: So, Toney Jackson never recorded, and I'm very curious about what he sounded like.

Well, he sounded pretty good as a piano player, as far as I could judge, at the time, because I -- at the time I was more involved with my work, and my work was not exactly straight playing. Both, you see.
With Dad Cook you had to, because he'd give you some embellishments, with his body, and you'd have to make lip slides. You know what that is?

So, you see, so with my straight formation, I was advised to follow, and immediately follow the embellishment as he gives it. You see, his facial expressions, his expressions with his anatomy, you understand what he means, and you do one of those things and you know what he means --- ah, nah, ah, ah, ah, you see. And I really -- what was my point, you see, I'm traveling a little.
Well, how some of these fellows like Toney Jackson was saying, you say you were concentrating --
Yes, Toney Jackson, I think he was a very -- that is Mazie Mullins and Frank Wathers, they think he was terrific,

Dad Cook, naturally he -- as long as you have a feeling, you're okay with him. You must have heart. If you have no heart, you're no good, you see. Regardless of all the tuition you may have, if you don't have feeling, you're no good.
He was a fine man. A wonderful man.
